observation.visible_scene: A single dancer is filmed from behind in a bright white dance studio with a full-height mirror on the right wall. She wears a beige cap over long dark hair, a black sleeveless top, black shorts, a colorful patterned sash hanging at her right hip, black knee-high socks with white stripes, and black sneakers. The mirror shows her front (face, a light graphic tee, and mirrored arm/leg positions). The ceiling track lights, wall-mounted AC unit, white curtain, and a zigzag white frame on the floor remain fixed, indicating a static camera. The dancer is mid-movement throughout, performing arm gestures, weight shifts, and a gradual body turn.
visible_changes: The dancer's outer arm alternates between a fully extended horizontal reach (e.g. frames 1-3, 13-16, 27-31) and a bent, folded position near the hip/waist (e.g. frames 5-12, 17-20, 33-41), with the hand making small open/closed gestures.
Her torso rotates progressively from a straight back-on orientation to a right-side profile facing the mirror (clear by frames 25-41).
She shifts weight between feet with small steps and occasional foot lifts (e.g. left foot raised in frame 1, foot taps around frames 8-9, 19-22), accompanied by hip sway.
The colorful sash at her hip swings and trails with the body motion, its position changing frame to frame.
The mirror reflection reproduces every change as a front view: face visible, the same arm extensions and folds, and the same leg/hip shifts, confirming one person rather than two.
outside_clip_unknowns: The beginning and end of the choreography (both crop boundaries fall mid-phrase; motion is already underway at frame 1 and continues past frame 41).
The music, count, or intended dance phrase driving the gestures.
Any movement before or after this excerpt.
uncertain_details: Exact left/right labeling of the gesturing arm is ambiguous because the mirror flips the view; only the visible arm motion is described.
Camera is assumed static based on unchanged background geometry, but no independent parallax evidence is available.
Whether a foot lift is a step, a tap, or a balance shift cannot be resolved from sampled frames alone.
